Chapter 7: Revolution and the Fall of Empires.
As the Great War dragged on, the old order began to crumble. In Russia, the pressure became too much to bear. People who had already endured years of hardship and sacrifice just couldn’t take it anymore. They lost faith in their rulers. Nicholas, clinging to his belief in a divine mission, simply didn’t see the warning signs—until everything unraveled.
In the harsh winter of 1917, revolution erupted in the streets of Petrograd. Soldiers turned against their commanders, workers walked out in protest, and suddenly, the government collapsed. Nicholas had no choice but to step down, ending over three centuries of Romanov rule in the blink of an eye.
What happened next was both shocking and, in many ways, unavoidable. Nicholas and his family found themselves under house arrest. Their world shrank to just a handful of rooms and a few loyal servants. Imagine that: one day, you’re the most powerful person in Russia... and the next, you’re a prisoner of your own history. Nicholas wrote desperate letters to his cousin George, hoping for help or even just a way out. But the British government hesitated, worried about public backlash and the risks of getting involved. The bond between the cousins, so strong in happier times, was now no match for the tide of revolution and war.
Meanwhile, things weren’t much better in Germany. The war had brought nothing but hardship and disappointment. People who had once cheered for their Kaiser now blamed him for everything they’d lost. As the war neared its end, Berlin was gripped by its own revolution. Soldiers and workers demanded peace, and the monarchy just couldn’t hold on. Wilhelm, facing the collapse of his empire, slipped away into exile in the Netherlands. He’d dreamed of glory and greatness, but ended up alone, haunted by what might have been.
Only George managed to weather the storm. The British monarchy, though battered, survived the chaos. George understood that survival meant embracing change. He backed reforms, helped extend voting rights, and worked hard to show the royal family as a symbol of unity for the nation. The old ways were gone, but the monarchy itself endured—reshaped by the fires of war.
But the end of the war didn’t bring much relief. The world was left with scars—loss, grief, and uncertainty everywhere you looked. The ancient empires that had once ruled over Europe simply vanished, replaced by new countries and fresh doubts. Those cousins, who’d once inherited lives of privilege and power, suddenly found themselves relics of a world that no longer existed.
Here’s something to think about: history rarely gives out second chances. The choices that get made in those critical moments—when people hesitate or misjudge, or just can’t see what’s coming—those decisions can’t ever be undone. For all their hopes and ambitions, the cousins were swept away by forces so much bigger than themselves.
